root.note: šabbāṯ. Some trace it further to Akkadian šapattum, but that link is uncertain.

history: The Portuguese week is unusual: from Monday to Friday the days have numbers, segunda-feira to sexta-feira. Only the weekend has names, and both are religious. Sábado comes from Hebrew shabbat, ‘rest’, the Jewish day of rest. Greek made it sábbaton, Church Latin sabbatum, and Portuguese kept it as the name of Saturday. Domingo, Sunday, is the Lord's day, Latin dies dominicus. English Saturday went the other way and kept the Roman god Saturn. Spanish sábado and Italian sabato share the Hebrew origin. In Portuguese the days are written with a small letter, and the stress falls on the first syllable: no sábado, ‘on Saturday’.
historyEinfach: Sábado means ‘Saturday’. The word comes from Hebrew shabbat, ‘rest’. It is the Jewish day of rest. Greek and Latin took the word, and it came to Portuguese. English Saturday is different: it is the day of the Roman god Saturn. Portuguese writes the days with a small letter: o sábado.

elsewhere.text: The Hebrew word for the day of rest reached Portuguese through Greek and Latin.
English took its Saturday from the Roman god, not from the day of rest.
